strengths: ELSA delivers substantial reported improvements at high sparsity across multiple architectures and scales. At 90% sparsity on LLaMA-2-7B, C4 perplexity improves from ALPS's 180.9 to 23.14, with corresponding improvements in average downstream accuracy.
The evaluation covers two perplexity datasets, seven downstream tasks, unstructured and semi-structured sparsity, and models up to 27B parameters. Detailed numerical results accompany the main plots.

The objective-aware projection has a useful controlled ablation: at 90% sparsity on LLaMA-3.2-3B, it reduces perplexity from 65.41 to 48.69. The low-precision implementation also offers a practical direction for reducing optimization memory.
weaknesses: The main comparisons do not isolate the proposed method from additional training and data. Baselines receive 128 calibration sequences, whereas ELSA performs 4,096 optimization steps with batch size 8 and larger datasets. Missing comparisons include pruning followed by matched next-token fine-tuning and iterative magnitude pruning under equivalent data and compute budgets. The objective ablation on OPT-125M alone does not resolve this confound.

The convergence guarantees do not cover the implemented algorithm. Appendix Algorithm 1 uses Euclidean projection, constant penalty, and an unusually restrictive inner-solve condition; experiments use Fisher-weighted projection, stochastic Adam, scheduled penalties, and quantized auxiliary states. Changing only the projection metric does not preserve the stated Euclidean ADMM derivation. No argument establishes that the practical updates satisfy the proof's conditions or that quantization errors vanish as required.

The proof itself contains a substantive error: Theorem A.4 assumes the sparsity constraint set S is finite and therefore extracts eventually constant projected iterates. The set of real-valued vectors with at most k nonzeros is infinite. Moreover, stationarity of limit points does not establish convergence of the full sequence or attainment of an optimal solution, despite stronger claims in the text.

Claims of retaining high fidelity or avoiding significant degradation at 90% sparsity are overstated. LLaMA-2-7B C4 perplexity increases from 7.26 to 23.14 and average downstream accuracy falls from 59.67% to 38.52%. ELSA also underperforms leading baselines at 50–60% sparsity and does not establish an advantage for semi-structured sparsity. The evidence supports improved recovery relative to collapsing baselines, rather than near-preservation of dense-model capabilities.

The novelty is insufficiently established relative to existing end-to-end pruning and ADMM-based neural-network compression. Variable splitting, hard-thresholding projection, and low-precision state storage are established techniques. Comparisons with relevant training-based approaches, including the cited MaskLLM and ProxSparse for semi-structured sparsity, are absent.

Efficiency and reproducibility evidence is incomplete. There are no measured pruning runtimes, GPU-hours, inference speedups, or detailed peak-memory comparisons supporting the practical efficiency discussion. The code links are blank, the main training-set size and practical update procedure are incompletely specified, and no variability estimates are reported. Numerical inconsistencies also require correction: Section 5.1 reports OPT-125M perplexities of 42.99 and 47.45 where Table 6 gives 34.32 and 47.74, and reports LLaMA-2-13B perplexity of 27.84 where Table 6 gives 25.07.

strengths: ELSA delivers substantial reported improvements at high sparsity across several model families and sizes. At 90% sparsity on LLaMA-2-7B, C4 perplexity is 23.14 versus ALPS’s 180.9, and average downstream accuracy improves from 32.03% to 38.52%. These are meaningful gains over the evaluated baselines.

The evaluation covers two perplexity datasets, seven downstream tasks, multiple sparsity levels, and extensions to semi-structured and non-uniform sparsity. The 27B experiment provides useful evidence of implementation scalability.

The objective-aware projection has a useful controlled ablation: on LLaMA-3.2-3B at 90% sparsity, it reduces perplexity from 65.41 to 48.69. Reusing optimizer statistics is also an appealing implementation choice.
weaknesses: The main comparisons confound algorithmic improvements with substantially greater optimization and data budgets. Baselines receive 128 calibration sequences, whereas ELSA performs 4,096 training steps with batch size 8. There are no matched-budget comparisons against pruning followed by next-token fine-tuning, gradual magnitude pruning, or projected-gradient training. Consequently, the results do not establish how much improvement comes specifically from ADMM or abandoning reconstruction objectives. The objective ablation on OPT-125M alone does not resolve this.

The convergence proof contains a concrete mathematical error. Appendix A, Theorem A.4 assumes that the sparsity constraint set S is finite and therefore that a convergent subsequence eventually has constant sparse iterates. However, S = {x in R^d : ||x||_0 <= k} is infinite; finitely many support patterns do not imply finitely many parameter vectors. The stated proof is therefore invalid as written.

The analyzed algorithm does not cover the implemented method. Algorithm 1 uses Euclidean projection before the x-update and requires a particular quantized optimality equation and relative-error condition. The practical method uses Fisher-weighted projection, iterative Adam updates, quantized auxiliary storage, and a varying penalty schedule. The paper does not establish the required error condition or extend the analysis to these modifications. Even a corrected limit-point stationarity result would not justify claims of convergence to an optimal solution of Equation (1).

Claims of preserving fidelity 'without significant performance degradation' are contradicted by the absolute results. At 90% sparsity, LLaMA-2-7B C4 perplexity rises from 7.26 to 23.14 and average task accuracy falls from 59.67% to 38.52%. ELSA also frequently underperforms existing methods at 50–60% sparsity; for 2:4 sparsity, its average accuracy is 49.59% versus ALPS’s 53.85%. The supported conclusion is improved high-sparsity recovery, not near-lossless extreme compression.

The methodological novelty is insufficiently established. The core construction is standard sparsity-constrained ADMM, supplemented with diagonal gradient statistics and established low-precision storage techniques. The paper needs stronger positioning against end-to-end pruning and retraining approaches, and direct evidence that ADMM improves over simpler optimization methods under equivalent budgets.

Efficiency claims lack adequate measurements. The paper reports neither pruning wall-clock time nor comparative GPU-hours, measured peak memory, or inference speedups. The stated 66% memory reduction is not accompanied by a detailed measurement breakdown or a matched full-precision quality comparison. Running the largest experiments on four H200 GPUs demonstrates feasibility, but does not establish a favorable resource–quality tradeoff.

Reproducibility and reporting require correction. Code-release locations are blank, the main ELSA training-set size is not explicitly specified, and seed variability is unreported. Section 5.1 gives OPT-125M perplexities of 42.99 and 47.45 where Table 6 lists 34.32 and 47.74, and reports LLaMA-2-13B perplexity of 27.84 where the table lists 25.07. The claim of highest accuracy on six of seven tasks at 90% sparsity also does not match Table 7: ELSA leads five, with ARC-C and RTE led by other methods.

strengths: The high-sparsity improvements over the evaluated baselines are substantial and consistent across several architectures and sizes. At 90% sparsity, LLaMA-2-7B achieves C4 perplexity of 23.14 versus 180.9 for ALPS, and average downstream accuracy of 38.52% versus 32.63% for the strongest reported baseline.

Directly optimizing the language-modeling objective is well motivated. The objective-aware projection has useful empirical support: on LLaMA-3.2-3B at 90% sparsity, it improves perplexity from 65.41 to 48.69.

The experiments cover multiple sparsity levels, two perplexity datasets, seven downstream tasks, and alternative sparsity patterns. The low-precision implementation also demonstrates feasibility on a 27B model.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not isolate the proposed method's contribution from additional training and data. Baselines receive 128 calibration sequences, whereas ELSA uses larger datasets and 4,096 gradient steps with batch size 8. There are no matched-budget comparisons against pruning followed by language-model fine-tuning, gradual magnitude pruning, or projected-gradient optimization. The objective ablation on OPT-125M alone does not resolve this central confound.

The convergence claims are not established for the implemented method. Appendix A analyzes Euclidean projection with stringent subproblem accuracy conditions, while practical ELSA uses an evolving Fisher-weighted projection, stochastic Adam updates, and often a changing penalty. The analysis also does not cover the implemented quantization of both auxiliary states. Moreover, the proof of Theorem A.4 incorrectly assumes that the real-valued sparsity constraint set S is finite. These are substantive gaps, and limit-point stationarity would not establish convergence to an optimal solution.

The central claim of preserving high fidelity with little degradation at 90% sparsity overstates the results. For LLaMA-2-7B, C4 perplexity increases from 7.26 to 23.14 and average downstream accuracy falls from 59.67% to 38.52%. ELSA substantially improves on collapsing baselines, but still loses considerable capability. It also underperforms leading baselines at 50–60% sparsity and does not establish an advantage for N:M sparsity.

Novelty is insufficiently positioned relative to prior end-to-end ADMM neural-network pruning and pruning with retraining. The underlying constrained formulation and variable splitting are standard; stronger comparisons are needed to establish what the proposed combination contributes beyond applying established optimization tools to LLMs.

Practical efficiency is insufficiently evaluated. The paper reports neither pruning runtime nor GPU-hours, and provides no measured inference latency, throughput, or sparse-storage costs. The claimed 66% memory reduction lacks a detailed peak-memory comparison, and there is no controlled ELSA versus ELSA-L quality comparison at the same model size.

Reporting and reproducibility need improvement. Section 5.1 gives perplexities inconsistent with Table 6, including 27.84 versus 25.07 for LLaMA-2-13B at 90% sparsity. The claim of winning six of seven downstream tasks at 90% sparsity also contradicts Table 7. Code links are blank, exact main-experiment dataset sizes and practical update details are incomplete, and variability across runs is not reported.

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: preserving LLM quality at high unstructured sparsity. Optimizing the language-modeling objective jointly across layers is well motivated.

Reports substantial high-sparsity improvements across several model families and sizes. At 90% sparsity, LLaMA-2-7B achieves C4 perplexity 23.14 versus 180.9 for ALPS, with additional evaluations on WikiText-2 and seven downstream tasks.

The matched-data retraining comparison provides meaningful supporting evidence: ELSA improves over Wanda plus full fine-tuning from 34.87 to 23.14 C4 perplexity at 90% sparsity with similar reported compute.

Includes actual deployment measurements, a 27B-model experiment, and a useful projection ablation. The reported inference speedups and memory savings demonstrate practical potential beyond parameter-count reductions.
weaknesses: The convergence proof has a substantive mathematical error. Appendix A asserts that the sparsity constraint set S is finite and uses this to obtain eventually constant projected iterates. However, S = {v in R^d: ||v||_0 <= k} is infinite. Consequently, the supplied argument does not establish the claimed theorem. Moreover, stationarity of limit points is weaker than convergence of the entire sequence or obtaining an optimal solution.

The theoretical algorithm differs materially from the implemented method. Algorithm 1 uses Euclidean projection, constant penalty, and a restrictive subproblem-error condition; experiments use Fisher-weighted projection, stochastic Adam updates, and a changing penalty. The proof also does not model quantization of z as described in Section 3.3. No argument establishes that fixed-precision storage satisfies the required vanishing relative-error condition. Thus, the guarantees do not substantiate the practical ELSA/ELSA-L algorithms.

Most headline comparisons are confounded by training resources: ELSA uses 32,768 sequences versus 128 for the principal baselines, a 256-fold data difference. The Wanda retraining comparison partially addresses this, but stronger pruning initializations followed by matched retraining, gradual pruning, and projected-gradient baselines are missing. The evidence does not adequately isolate ADMM's contribution from end-to-end training and additional data.

Claims of preserving high fidelity or avoiding significant degradation are contradicted by the dense-model comparisons. At 90% sparsity, LLaMA-2-7B C4 perplexity increases from 7.26 to 23.14 and average downstream accuracy falls from 59.67% to 38.52%. LLaMA-2-13B accuracy falls from 63.02% to 37.37%. These are substantial losses despite improvements over other pruners; downstream usability at 95–99% sparsity is not demonstrated.

Novelty is insufficiently established relative to existing optimization-based pruning. The central construction combines standard ADMM, hard thresholding, an Adam-derived importance metric, and low-precision states. The manuscript needs stronger positioning against prior end-to-end ADMM pruning and controlled comparisons showing why this particular combination is necessary.

Figure 3 constructs a common perplexity–parameter Pareto frontier across model families with different tokenizers. Token-level perplexities are not directly comparable across tokenizations, so this figure does not establish the claimed cross-family frontier. Comparisons should use a common normalized likelihood measure or remain within compatible model families.

Reproducibility and reporting need improvement. The practical update schedule and final sparse-model extraction are insufficiently specified, retraining-baseline hyperparameters are absent, and results lack seed variability. Section 5.1 also conflicts with Table 10: OPT-125M ELSA C4 perplexities at 60%/80% are reported as 42.99/47.45 versus 33.22/47.74, and LLaMA-2-13B at 90% as 27.84 versus 25.07.

strengths: The high-sparsity perplexity improvements are substantial and consistent across several architectures and model sizes. At 90% sparsity on LLaMA-2-7B, ELSA achieves C4 perplexity 23.14 versus 180.9 for ALPS.

The paper includes meaningful retraining controls: with matched training data, Wanda plus full fine-tuning reaches C4 perplexity 34.87 versus ELSA's 23.14. This provides evidence beyond comparisons with inexpensive one-shot pruning.

Deployment measurements demonstrate practical benefits on an RTX 3090, including 2.56× throughput and 4.60× memory reduction at 90% sparsity. The projection ablation and 27B experiment provide additional useful evidence.
weaknesses: The convergence proof contains a substantive error: Theorem A.4 assumes that the sparsity constraint set S is finite and therefore that a convergent subsequence eventually has identical projected values. S = {x in R^d: ||x||_0 ≤ k} is infinite; finitely many supports do not imply finitely many parameter vectors. The proof does not establish the stated guarantee as written.

The theory does not cover the implemented method. Appendix A analyzes Euclidean projection, a constant penalty, and an x-update satisfying a stringent vanishing relative-error condition. Experiments use Fisher-weighted projection, stochastic Adam, scheduled penalties, and quantized auxiliary states. No argument establishes the required error condition for the proposed quantizer. Moreover, replacing only the z-update's metric means it no longer minimizes the augmented Lagrangian in Equation 6, invalidating a direct appeal to standard ADMM descent.

Claims of preserving fidelity without significant degradation are contradicted by the absolute results. At 90% sparsity, LLaMA-2-7B WikiText perplexity rises from 5.47 to 26.97, while average downstream accuracy falls from 59.67% to 38.52%. LLaMA-2-13B accuracy falls from 63.02% to 37.37%. These are meaningful improvements over failing baselines, but substantial losses relative to dense models. No downstream evaluation establishes usability at 95–99% sparsity.

The main comparisons confound optimization strategy with data and training budget: ELSA uses 32,768 sequences versus 128 for the principal baselines, a 256-fold difference. The matched-data Wanda retraining controls partially address this, but stronger retrained baselines and budget-matched iterative pruning or projected-gradient methods are missing. The objective ablation is limited to OPT-125M and leaves the REM implementation insufficiently specified.

Methodological novelty is insufficiently established. The core construction combines standard sparsity-constrained ADMM, an existing Adam-based Fisher approximation, and established low-precision state storage. Positioning against prior end-to-end ADMM neural-network pruning is inadequate, and the experiments do not isolate the advantage of ADMM over simpler end-to-end sparse optimization.

Several reporting inconsistencies undermine confidence. Section 5.1 reports LLaMA-2-13B C4 perplexity 27.84 at 90% sparsity, whereas Table 10 gives 25.07. The claim of winning six of seven downstream tasks at 90% sparsity conflicts with Table 11, which shows five wins. Reproduction links are blank, and important details such as excluded parameters, achieved whole-model sparsity, and retraining-baseline hyperparameters are insufficiently specified.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: preserving LLM quality at very high sparsity. Optimizing the language-modeling objective jointly across layers is a sensible alternative to independent reconstruction objectives.

The reported high-sparsity improvements are substantial and span several architectures and scales. At 90% sparsity, LLaMA-2-7B achieves C4 perplexity 23.14 versus 180.9 for ALPS. The comparison with Wanda plus full fine-tuning is particularly useful: ELSA improves perplexity from 34.87 to 23.14 at similar reported compute cost.

The evaluation includes two perplexity datasets, seven downstream tasks, pruning costs, and actual inference measurements. The reported 3.98× throughput improvement and 7.80× memory reduction at 95% sparsity provide practical evidence beyond parameter counts.

The projection ablation supports the proposed weighting heuristic: at 90% sparsity on LLaMA-3.2-3B, perplexity improves from 65.41 to 48.69. The 27B experiment also demonstrates useful implementation effort.
weaknesses: The convergence guarantees do not establish correctness of the implemented method. Appendix A analyzes Euclidean projection with a constant penalty and restrictive subproblem-error conditions, whereas the implementation uses Adam-weighted projection, stochastic optimization, scheduled penalties, and quantized auxiliary states. Algorithm 1 does not model the stated quantization of z. No argument establishes that the practical updates satisfy its error conditions.

The proof contains a concrete invalid assumption: Theorem A.4 treats S as finite and concludes that a convergent subsequence of sparse vectors eventually becomes constant. The defined set S = {v in R^d: ||v||_0 <= k} is infinite. Moreover, conditional stationarity of limit points would not establish convergence to an optimal solution, as suggested elsewhere in the paper.

The main comparison confounds the optimization method with substantially greater training data and access to end-to-end updates: ELSA uses 32,768 sequences versus 128 for reconstruction baselines, a 256× difference. The matched-data Wanda retraining experiment partially addresses this, but only for one model and a limited baseline family. Comparisons with stronger pruning initializations followed by retraining, gradual pruning, and projected-gradient or conventional ADMM training under matched budgets are needed to isolate the contribution.

Claims of preserving high fidelity or avoiding significant degradation are inconsistent with the absolute results. At 90% sparsity, LLaMA-2-7B C4 perplexity increases from 7.26 to 23.14, and average downstream accuracy falls from 59.67% to 38.52%. For LLaMA-2-13B, accuracy falls from 63.02% to 37.37%. These are meaningful improvements over collapsing baselines, but substantial losses relative to the dense models. Downstream usability at 95–99% sparsity is not established.

Novelty is insufficiently separated from established end-to-end ADMM pruning and sparse retraining. The main formulation is standard, while diagonal weighting and low-precision state storage are familiar techniques. The paper needs stronger positioning and controlled comparisons demonstrating what its particular combination contributes. Adam's second moments are also not generally equivalent to the empirical Fisher or Gauss–Newton matrix, especially when gradients include the ADMM penalty.

Reproducibility and reporting need improvement. The code and environment links are absent, the practical update procedure and treatment of excluded parameters are insufficiently specified, and repeated-run uncertainty is not reported. Section 5.1 also gives perplexities inconsistent with Table 10, including 27.84 versus 25.07 for LLaMA-2-13B at 90% sparsity. These issues, together with the theoretical and comparison gaps, prevent the promising empirical results from meeting the acceptance threshold.
